name: Brepocitinib

card.summary: An oral TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor studied for autoimmune conditions, including alopecia areata and scarring alopecias, where regrowth of hair is the appearance-relevant outcome.
card.note: Prescription immunomodulator; JAK inhibitors as a class carry warnings on infections, clots and malignancy.

quick.overview:
Brepocitinib is an oral, once-daily drug that blocks two enzymes in the JAK family, TYK2 and JAK1, which relay inflammatory cytokine signals including interferons, IL-12 and IL-23.[2] It was developed for autoimmune disease and has been tested in dermatomyositis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, hidradenitis suppurativa and hair-loss conditions.

For looks, the relevant use is autoimmune hair loss. A phase 2a trial tested it alongside ritlecitinib in alopecia areata, and a separate phase 2a trial tested it in scarring (cicatricial) alopecias such as lichen planopilaris.[8][7] Its main approval is for adult dermatomyositis, a condition with skin rash and muscle weakness; Wikipedia reports a US approval in August 2026.[11]
quick.how: It is a prescription medicine taken by mouth under specialist care, and in trials is compared with placebo over periods of 24 to 52 weeks. It is not a cosmetic product and is not used for ordinary pattern hair loss. Online discussion is limited and centers on interest in JAK inhibitors for alopecia areata generally.
quick.risks: Reported adverse reactions include upper respiratory infection, headache, fatigue, urinary tract infection and nausea.[11] Reviews of JAK-pathway drugs describe class concerns about infections, venous thromboembolism and malignancy, which TYK2-selective agents may partly differ on.[4][3] It is Rx-only and requires medical monitoring.

lead: Brepocitinib (code name PF-06700841) is an oral TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor.[2][3] By blocking these kinases it reduces signaling by type I and II interferons, IL-12 and IL-23, pathways implicated in several autoimmune and inflammatory skin and hair diseases.[2][3]

In autoimmune hair loss, immune cells attack the hair follicle; the aim of treatment is to calm that attack so hair can regrow. Brepocitinib was tested for alopecia areata in a phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled study with ritlecitinib,[8] and for cicatricial alopecias including lichen planopilaris in a 52-week phase 2a trial.[7]

Its first marketed indication is dermatomyositis in adults. A phase 3 trial of 241 patients reported superiority of the 30 mg dose over placebo on the Total Improvement Score.[6] Wikipedia reports FDA approval in August 2026 under the brand Lisraya.[11]

chain: Reduces immune attack on hair follicles
Hair may regrow in alopecia areata or slow scarring in cicatricial alopecia
angle.text: For people whose hair loss is autoimmune, brepocitinib was studied as a way to quiet the inflammation damaging follicles. It is not aimed at common androgenetic hair loss.

paras: The phase 3 VALOR trial in dermatomyositis compared brepocitinib 30 mg, 15 mg and placebo for 52 weeks in 241 adults; the mean Total Improvement Score at week 52 was 46.5, 37.5 and 31.2 respectively.[6] Wikipedia lists dermatomyositis as the approved indication.[11]

Phase 2a trials examined alopecia areata[8] and cicatricial alopecia,[7] and earlier trials examined plaque psoriasis,[9] psoriatic arthritis[10] and hidradenitis suppurativa.[12] Psoriasis reviews note brepocitinib among JAK-pathway agents under investigation.[5][4]

TYK2 participates in signaling downstream of type I interferons, IL-12, IL-23 and IL-10, and a review notes it has a distinct set of immune effects from JAK1, JAK2 and JAK3.[3] Brepocitinib inhibits TYK2 and JAK1, reducing signaling by IFN-alpha/beta, IL-12, IL-23 and IFN-gamma.[2] Some reviewers suggest TYK2 inhibitors may have a safety profile that differs from broader JAK inhibitors.[3]

Common adverse reactions reported for the approved use include upper respiratory tract infection, headache, fatigue, urinary tract infection and nausea.[11] Reviews of JAK inhibitors in immune-mediated disease have raised class concerns about infections, venous thromboembolism and malignancy.[4]

A phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluated oral ritlecitinib and brepocitinib in alopecia areata with 24-week results.[8] A 52-week phase 2a randomized trial examined brepocitinib in cicatricial alopecias, including lichen planopilaris.[7] Other phase 2 trials covered plaque psoriasis,[9] psoriatic arthritis[10] and hidradenitis suppurativa,[12] and the NEJM phase 3 trial covered dermatomyositis.[6] Detailed hair outcomes are in the trial publications.

Brepocitinib was developed first within Pfizer under the code PF-06700841 and later by Priovant Therapeutics, a Roivant company, according to Wikipedia's account of the approval.[11] It received orphan drug and priority review designations.[11] It is prescription-only.

timeline.event: Phase IIa plaque psoriasis trial published.[9]
Phase 2a alopecia areata results (24 weeks) published.[8]
Phase IIb psoriatic arthritis trial published.[10]
Phase 3 dermatomyositis trial published; FDA approval reported for dermatomyositis.[6][11]
